claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by grain boundary sliding.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten-based fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by grain boundary sliding.
Elevated temperatures weaken grain boundary cohesion.
Weakening of grain boundary cohesion makes grain boundary sliding pronounced at high temperature.
Introducing controlled grain-boundary precipitates strengthens grain boundaries.
Strengthening grain boundaries with precipitates impedes grain boundary sliding.
Grain boundary sliding is the dominant deformation mode in the proposed tungsten-based alloy at 1000–1500°C.
Grain boundary sliding increases high-temperature plastic strain.
Precipitate-reinforced grain boundaries reduce grain boundary sliding.
Grain-boundary precipitates provide a barrier to crack initiation and propagation.
Reducing grain boundary sliding through precipitate reinforcement enhances toughness.
Relative to an unmodified control, precipitate-reinforced specimens will exhibit lower plastic strain during high-temperature mechanical loading.
Relative to an unmodified control, precipitate-reinforced specimens will exhibit higher toughness during high-temperature mechanical loading.
The unmodified tungsten-based baseline undergoes significant grain boundary sliding under high-temperature loading.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to tungsten-based plasma-facing alloys operating between 1000°C and 1500°C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to substantially different material systems or temperature regimes in which other deformation mechanisms dominate.
